title: What Are the 7 Rs of Fashion? Meaning and Practical Steps
h1: The 7 Rs of sustainable fashion: what they are and how to practise each one
excerpt: What are the 7 Rs of fashion? Reduce, reuse, repair, repurpose, rent, resell and recycle, why lists differ, and practical steps for each, in order of impact.
tldr: The 7 Rs of fashion are usually reduce, reuse, repair, repurpose, rent, resell and recycle, though some lists use rethink, refuse or rot. Buying less and rewearing what you own make the biggest difference; recycling is the last resort because textile-to-textile recycling remains below 1%.
body:
The 7 Rs of fashion are most often given as reduce, reuse, repair, repurpose, rent, resell and recycle: seven habits that keep clothes in use for longer and out of landfill. There's no official list, though. Some versions swap in rethink, refuse, rewear, reject or rot. Every version agrees on the order that matters most: buying less and wearing what you have come first, and recycling comes last.

What are the 7 Rs of fashion?

The 7 Rs grew out of the older "reduce, reuse, recycle". The extra Rs fill in what happens between buying a garment and throwing it away. The most common set, used by the Canadian non-profit Fashion Takes Action, is:

  1. Reduce: buy fewer new clothes.
  2. Reuse: keep clothes in circulation by rewearing, swapping, borrowing and buying secondhand.
  3. Repair: fix damage instead of replacing the item.
  4. Repurpose: turn something you won't wear into something you will use.
  5. Rent: hire clothes for one-off occasions.
  6. Resell: pass on clothes you don't wear to someone who will.
  7. Recycle: send clothes that are beyond use to be turned back into fibre.

Why sources list different Rs

The 7 Rs are a teaching tool rather than a standard, so organisations and writers pick the seven that suit their message. Three published versions:

SourceTheir 7 Rs
Fashion Takes ActionReduce, reuse, repair, repurpose, rent, resell, recycle
TRVSTRethink, refuse, reduce, reuse, repair, recycle, rot (with research as an extra R)
Eluxe MagazineReduce, reuse, repurpose, recycle, repair, reject, rent

The differences are smaller than they look. Rethink, refuse and reject are all about not buying in the first place, so they sit naturally under reduce. Rewear is the everyday half of reuse. Rot (composting natural fibres) is an end-of-life option next to recycling. This guide uses the Fashion Takes Action list and folds the others in where they fit.

The 7 Rs in practice, in order of impact

Most lists present the Rs in no particular order. Here they're ranked roughly by how much difference each makes, following the same logic as the EU's waste hierarchy, in which preventing waste is the preferred option and landfill the last resort (European Commission).

1. Reduce (including rethink and refuse)

Every other R deals with clothes that already exist. Reduce is the only one that stops a garment being made. The Ellen MacArthur Foundation reports that clothing production roughly doubled over 15 years while the number of times a garment is worn fell by almost 40% (Ellen MacArthur Foundation).

  • Keep a wishlist and buy only what's still on it after 30 days.
  • Before buying, name three outfits the new piece would make with clothes you already own. If you can't, skip it.
  • Unsubscribe from sale emails and mute shopping accounts you follow mostly out of habit.
  • Refuse freebies you won't wear, like promotional T-shirts and event merchandise.
  • For things you do buy, a simple test such as the 30 wear rule keeps quality ahead of quantity.

2. Reuse (including rewear and secondhand)

The most sustainable clothes are usually the ones you already own. WRAP's 2022 research found the average UK adult hadn't worn about a quarter of their clothes for at least a year (WRAP), so most wardrobes have plenty to rewear.

  • Repeat outfits on purpose. Nobody keeps track as closely as you think.
  • Shop secondhand first: charity shops, vintage stores and resale apps.
  • Go to a clothes swap, or set one up with friends.
  • Borrow for things you'll wear once, from a friend or family member.

A capsule wardrobe is one practical way to build rewearing into daily life, because every piece is chosen to work with the rest. A digital wardrobe app can help too, by showing you what you already own. FitWardrobe is our app, and it isn't available yet; it suggests outfits only from clothes you've photographed.

3. Repair

Repair keeps a garment you already like in use for longer. WRAP says that repairing an item typically extends its life by a further 1.3 years (WRAP).

  • Learn the three repairs that cover most problems: sewing on a button, closing a split seam and darning a small hole in knitwear.
  • Take bigger jobs to a tailor (zips, hems, relining) and shoes to a cobbler for new heels or soles.
  • Use a fabric shaver on pilled jumpers. It takes ten minutes and makes them look far newer.
  • Find a Repair Café, a free meeting place where volunteers help you fix things, clothes included. There are over 2,500 worldwide (Repair Café).
  • Prevent damage: wash cooler, wash less often, follow the care label and air-dry where you can.

Keep a small basket for anything waiting to be mended, somewhere you'll see it. Repairs left at the back of a wardrobe tend never to happen.

4. Rent

Renting suits clothes you'd wear once or twice: formalwear for a wedding, a suit for an interview, ski gear for one trip a year. Suit and formalwear hire has existed for decades; online rental services now cover everyday and designer clothes in many countries.

  • Rent for occasions, not for everyday basics you'll wear weekly.
  • Check the service's cleaning, delivery and damage policies before you order.
  • For a local option, ask whether formalwear shops near you hire as well as sell.

5. Resell

If something's in good condition and you don't wear it, selling it keeps it in use and puts money back in your pocket. Resale apps such as Vinted, Depop and eBay operate in many countries, alongside local consignment shops.

  • Photograph items in daylight on a plain background, and include a close-up of the label.
  • Give measurements, not just the size on the label, and mention any flaws.
  • Sell a season ahead: coats in early autumn, linen in spring.

6. Repurpose

Repurposing gives a garment a new use without breaking it down. It's the right choice for things too worn to sell but too good to bin.

  • Cut worn T-shirts and cotton shirts into cleaning cloths.
  • Turn jeans with blown-out knees into shorts.
  • Keep fabric from old shirts as patches for future repairs.
  • Use a jumper that's shrunk in the wash as a dog bed lining or draught excluder.

7. Recycle (and rot)

Recycling comes last because so little clothing is turned back into clothing. The Ellen MacArthur Foundation says textile-to-textile recycling remains below 1%, and more than 80% of textile waste is still incinerated, landfilled or lost to the environment (Ellen MacArthur Foundation).

  • Recycle only what's genuinely beyond wearing: torn, stained or worn through.
  • Use textile banks or retailer take-back schemes rather than household rubbish bins, and ask what happens to the clothes.
  • Give wearable clothes to reuse routes such as charity shops instead.

Policy is moving the same way. The EU's 2025 revision of its Waste Framework Directive requires member states to set up producer responsibility schemes, so that textile makers contribute to handling used and waste textiles (European Commission).

Some lists add rot: composting clothes made entirely of natural, untreated fibres such as cotton, linen or wool. It only works if you remove synthetic thread, elastic, zips and buttons first, and many blends won't break down at all.

Which R matters most?

Reduce, then reuse. Wearing what you have for longer has a measurable effect: WRAP estimated that keeping clothes in active use for three months longer would cut each of their carbon, water and waste footprints by 5 to 10% (WRAP, 2012). Repair supports both. Renting and reselling are useful for specific items. Recycling matters, but at today's rates it can't make up for buying more.

A rough order to keep in mind: reduce, reuse, repair, rent or resell, repurpose, recycle.

How to start without overhauling everything

  1. This week: pull out everything you haven't worn in a year and sort it into wear again, mend, sell and recycle.
  2. This month: fix or take in the mend pile, and list the sell pile.
  3. For the next three months: buy nothing new except replacements for things that have worn out. If you want structure, Project 333 is a three-month limit on what you wear.
  4. Next occasion: rent, borrow or rewear before buying.

Pick the R that's easiest for you and start there. For most people that's rewearing what's already in the wardrobe.

faq.q: What are the 7 Rs of fashion?
faq.a: The most common list is reduce, reuse, repair, repurpose, rent, resell and recycle. They're habits for keeping clothes in use for longer and out of landfill. There's no official version, so some sources include rethink, refuse, rewear, reject or rot instead. All versions put buying less and wearing what you own first, and recycling last.

faq.q: Which of the 7 Rs of sustainable fashion is most important?
faq.a: Reduce. It's the only R that stops a garment being made, so it avoids the water, energy and materials used in production. Reuse comes next, because wearing clothes you already own for longer delays buying new ones. Recycling is the least effective, since textile-to-textile recycling remains below 1% according to the Ellen MacArthur Foundation.

faq.q: What is the difference between reuse, repurpose and recycle?
faq.a: Reuse keeps a garment as it is, worn again by you or someone else. Repurpose gives it a new job without breaking it down, such as turning a worn T-shirt into cleaning cloths. Recycle breaks the material down into fibre to make something new. Reuse saves the most, recycling the least, because each step loses more of the original garment.

It's better than throwing clothes away, but it works best for clean, wearable items that a charity shop can sell. Donate things someone would actually buy, and use textile banks or take-back schemes for damaged clothes instead. Selling or swapping good items yourself is often more reliable, because you know they're going to someone who wants them.

faq.q: What is the difference between the 3 Rs and the 7 Rs?
faq.a: The 3 Rs, reduce, reuse and recycle, are the original waste-reduction slogan. The 7 Rs of fashion keep those three and add steps specific to clothing, usually repair, repurpose, rent and resell. Some versions add rethink and refuse at the start, or rot at the end. The extra Rs cover what can happen to a garment before it's recycled.

faq.q: Can old clothes be recycled into new clothes?
faq.a: Only a tiny share are. The Ellen MacArthur Foundation says textile-to-textile recycling remains below 1%, and more than 80% of textile waste is incinerated, landfilled or lost. Blended fabrics are especially hard to separate. That's why recycling is the last of the 7 Rs, used for clothes that can't be worn, repaired, sold or repurposed.
